clue.text: Rental property close to ground now in a mess? That's disappointment

parts.note: a let is a property rented out to a tenant

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: last letter taken

indicators.note: something in a mess is jumbled up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rented house near the land is now a shambles, which is a big disappointment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to ground' gives D, and 'in a mess' rearranges NOW into OWN. LET is the British word for a rented property.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-down is an anticlimax or failure to meet expectations, a synonym for disappointment.

clue.text: Titled figure, one with old queen previously

parts.note: an earl holds a rank in the peerage, so he is a figure with a title
the Roman numeral for one
ER is the royal cipher Elizabeth Regina, and 'old' marks the reign as the last one rather than the present

explanation.surface: A nobleman standing beside somebody who used to be a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Two letters of royal shorthand carry the whole back end of this clue, and 'old' is not padding: it is what tells you which monarch's cipher is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: EARLIER and 'previously' both mean at a time before the one being talked about, and either can replace the other unchanged.

clue.text: Prepare article of clothing

definitions.meaning: the verb used of getting a wound, a salad or a shop window ready
the one-piece garment a woman puts on over her head

explanation.surface: An instruction to get a garment ready to wear.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves define, so the clue asserts nothing at all, and the join is invisible because 'Prepare article of clothing' reads as one sensible order.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb DRESS means to make ready — a wound, a salad, a window; as a noun it is the frock itself.

clue.text: Lose intensity with sport cancelled

parts.note: to sport a hat or a badge is to wear it where everyone can see
a match called off has been cancelled

explanation.surface: A fixture called off, and the excitement draining away with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sport' reads as a noun in the surface, a game, and it is a verb in the wordplay, the one used of wearing something conspicuously.
explanation.definitionFit: When a drug or an ache WEARS OFF its force fades away gradually, which is losing intensity.

clue.text: Plant if such to be cultivated by area

indicators.note: by means next to, so the area letter is set beside the rearranged letters
cultivated soil is turned over and worked, so the letters of if such are dug into a new order

explanation.surface: A gardening note: if a plant like this is to be grown, it needs a bit of space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be cultivated' looks like part of the gardening advice but it signals the shuffle of IF SUCH. The plant is named after the botanist Leonhart Fuchs, which fixes the awkward spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: A fuchsia is a flowering shrub with drooping purple, pink or red blossoms, a popular garden plant.

clue.text: Commotion from posh pair over thing for rowing

indicators.note: One thing sitting over another is written above it, and in a down entry above means earlier, so these letters go on top.

parts.note: U is the crossword's letter for upper class, from the U and non-U labels once given to posh and common usage
pr is the catalogue abbreviation for a pair
the blade you pull a boat along with

explanation.surface: Two well-bred people kicking up a din above somebody's boating gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' can mean quarrelling, which is where the surface points, and the wordplay wants the boating sense instead.
explanation.definitionFit: An UPROAR is a burst of loud confused noise and protest, which is what a commotion is.

clue.text: Eighth lad repaired feature of a car

indicators.note: Repairing something means taking its broken pieces and fitting them back together differently, which is what happens to these letters.

parts.note: nine letters of fodder, the two H's easy to lose count of

explanation.surface: The eighth boy in the line got a bit of somebody's car working again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Repaired' sits exactly where a solver expects a plain past tense, so the sentence reads as somebody fixing a car rather than as an instruction about letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A HEADLIGHT is one of the lamps at the front of a car, so the definition names it by the machine it belongs to.

clue.text: Source of sweet smell in faculty, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means as told by word of mouth, so the letters are what is heard

parts.note: IN followed by SENSE, since a sense such as smell is a faculty

explanation.surface: A sweet aroma is said to be noticeable in a university department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'faculty' looks like a university department, but here it is a sense, one of the body's faculties; IN SENSE said aloud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Incense is aromatic material burned to give off a fragrant smoke.

clue.text: A court could issue this direction over criminal

indicators.note: A criminal is someone who will not keep to the rules, and letters that will not keep to the rules of their spelling come out rearranged.

parts.note: thirteen letters of fodder, the preposition counting as letters like any other word

explanation.surface: A judge weighing up what instruction to hand down about an offender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over criminal' reads as 'concerning a wrongdoer', which hides the fact that both words are letters to be shuffled rather than sense to be followed.
explanation.definitionFit: An EVICTION ORDER is the instruction a court issues requiring an occupier to leave a property, so the opening phrase points straight at it.

clue.text: Impulse in abrupt removal of people after loss of power

indicators.note: Losing a thing means it is gone, so the letter named next comes out of the word rather than being added to it.

parts.note: a purge is a sudden clearing-out of unwanted people from a party or an office
P is the standard abbreviation for power, and it is the letter struck out

explanation.surface: A political clear-out happening the moment the leadership loses its grip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loss of power' reads as a government falling from office, which is the very same political story the first half of the clue is telling.
explanation.definitionFit: An URGE is a sudden strong wish to do something, the same inner push that 'impulse' names.

clue.text: Vacate Iran suffering turmoil in conflict

indicators.note: Turmoil is violent disorder, and whatever is suffering it does not keep its parts where they were.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, the verb and the country together

explanation.surface: People being told to leave Iran while the country is in upheaval.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a news bulletin, and the two words carrying the story — the order to leave and the country it applies to — are the letters themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people AT VARIANCE openly disagree with each other, which is what being in conflict describes.

clue.text: Debacle taking place in Sofia's condemned

indicators.note: Something taking place in a spot is sitting right there inside it, so the letters wanted are already present in the words that follow.

parts.note: six letters in a row, starting inside the first word and running on through the apostrophe into the second

explanation.surface: A disaster unfolding in Sofia, in a building that had already been condemned.
explanation.walkthrough: Sofia is the Bulgarian capital, so the sentence reads as a news report from abroad, and the possessive apostrophe does nothing but disguise the seam.
explanation.definitionFit: A FIASCO is a complete and humiliating failure, which is exactly what a debacle is.

clue.text: Repeated word, not new, linked to policy for conversational service

indicators.note: Putting this in front of a word cancels it, so the letter that word stands for comes out of the assembly instead of joining it.

parts.note: a chant is a phrase a crowd says over and over
N is the standard abbreviation for new, and it is the letter cancelled
a party's line is the policy it expects its members to take

explanation.surface: Somebody dropping a stale slogan and sticking to the official position instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The party line is worth filing away as an equation: 'policy', 'stance' or 'official position' will all turn into the same four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A CHATLINE is a phone or online service people ring up simply to talk to strangers, which makes it a conversational service.

clue.text: Commercial exhibition somehow rated reasonable

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters of rated are put into an unstated order

parts.note: fair means reasonable or just, as in a fair price

explanation.surface: A review of a commercial show that was somehow judged merely reasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rated reasonable' reads like a verdict on the show, but 'rated' is the anagram fodder and 'reasonable' a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade fair is a large exhibition where companies show and sell their products to the business world.

clue.text: Scandal is repressed by Dutch queen, perhaps

indicators.note: Something repressed is held down and kept out of sight, so this word ends up buried among the letters on either side of it.

parts.note: D is the standard abbreviation for Dutch
in bridge and whist the honours are the top cards — ace, king, queen, jack, ten — so a queen is one instance of one
the little word is taken straight off the page, letters and all

explanation.surface: A scandal being quietly hushed up by a Dutch monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the standard marker for definition by example: the queen is not the word wanted, only one of the things it covers.
explanation.definitionFit: DISHONOUR is the public disgrace attaching to someone whose wrongdoing comes out, which is what a scandal leaves behind.

clue.text: Correspond with a person keen on recycling, shortly

indicators.note: Saying a thing shortly is saying it cut short, so the word it follows gives up its final letter.

parts.note: the indefinite article supplies its own single letter
someone who champions recycling and conservation goes by this name, after the colour the environmental movement adopted

explanation.surface: Exchanging letters with an environmentally minded person before long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correspond' looks like writing letters, which is the picture the surface wants; the definition needs the other sense, of two accounts matching.
explanation.definitionFit: Two sets of figures that AGREE correspond with each other — the tallying sense of the word rather than the sense of getting on.

clue.text: Perform dental hygiene following feeling of deprivation

parts.note: f is the abbreviation printed in references to mean the page following
the ache of being deprived of somebody is a sense of loss

explanation.surface: Cleaning your teeth after a spell of feeling bereft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a joining word telling you which piece comes after which, and it is a piece in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: To FLOSS is to work waxed thread between the teeth, which is performing dental hygiene.

clue.text: Gents, maybe, with king appear largely for brief inspection

indicators.note: Taking most of a thing but not all of it is what this asks for, so the word it follows keeps everything except its final letter.

parts.note: the Gents is a British public lavatory, and loo is the everyday British word for one
K is the standard abbreviation for king, as on a playing card or a chess score sheet
to seem and to appear are the same verb, and the last letter of it goes

explanation.surface: The men's toilets and a king, by and large, turning up for a quick once-over.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the biggest hint here: a hyphenated four-and-three in a clue about a quick glance narrows the field hard before any parsing starts.
explanation.definitionFit: A LOOK-SEE is an informal quick glance at something to check it over, which is a brief inspection.

clue.text: Consider register by old military reserve at home

parts.note: to enter a name in a book is to register it
the TA was the Territorial Army, Britain's part-time volunteer reserve force, renamed in 2014
somebody at home is in

explanation.surface: Signing up with a former volunteer force without leaving the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The TA is worth filing away: 'volunteers', 'reserves' or 'territorials' in a British clue almost always want those two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To ENTERTAIN a proposal is to hold it in mind and give it a hearing without committing, which is exactly to consider it.

clue.text: Times shown by a court in Fenland place in a precise way

indicators.note: The small word is doing positional work: whatever is in a place sits inside it, so the pieces before it get planted within the letters that follow.

parts.note: Ely is the small cathedral city out in the Cambridgeshire fens
the multiplication sign, read aloud as 'times'
the article is taken at face value
ct is the abbreviation for Court used in street addresses

explanation.surface: The sitting times displayed by a courthouse somewhere out in the fens.
explanation.walkthrough: The Fens are the flat drained marshland of eastern England, and the cathedral city buried in this clue stands on what was once an island in them.
explanation.definitionFit: EXACTLY means with complete precision, so the adverb stands in for the phrase 'in a precise way' word for word.

clue.text: Small measure seen surprisingly to be huge

parts.note: one millimetre, written 1 mm, is a tiny measure; the 1 is read as the letter I

indicators.note: surprisingly means in an unexpected way, so the letters of seen turn up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A small measurement seen, against expectation, to be enormous.
explanation.walkthrough: The digit 1 in '1 mm' is read as the letter I, a common crossword trick, giving IMM.
explanation.definitionFit: Immense means extremely large or vast, so it is a straight synonym of huge.

clue.text: Like a checked report with appeal kept by two journalists

indicators.note: Something kept by somebody is held in their keeping, so this piece ends up shut inside the letters around it.

parts.note: ed is short for editor, and the clue asks for a pair of them side by side
IT is the crossword's shorthand for sex appeal

explanation.surface: Two newspapermen hanging on to the charm in a piece of writing.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex appeal comes from Elinor Glyn's 1927 novel and the It girl who followed it, and crosswords have kept the sense long after ordinary speech dropped it.
explanation.definitionFit: A report that has been EDITED has been gone over and corrected, so 'like a checked report' describes the state it is in.

clue.text: Absence of singer Stevie? Hardly a surprise!

parts.note: having an absence of something is having none of it
Stevie is only the forename; the wordplay wants the surname of the Motown singer and pianist

explanation.surface: Noticing that a famous soul singer has not turned up after all.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading 'Absence of' as an instruction rather than as part of the picture is the whole step, and the question mark is the setter owning up to the join.
explanation.definitionFit: 'NO WONDER' is what you say when an outcome was entirely predictable, which is what calling something hardly a surprise means.

clue.text: Take on a case for some about particular amount of money

indicators.note: A case is the shell round a thing rather than the thing itself, so only the outside letters of the word named are taken.

parts.note: the article is taken at face value

indicators.note: Something placed about a thing is wrapped round the outside of it, so these letters close over the piece that follows.

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word, which are its outside
a sum is a specified quantity of money

explanation.surface: A lawyer agreeing to act for a group of people in a dispute over money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is one of the setter's favourite words for the outside of something — a shell, a cover, a suitcase — and it never means the contents.
explanation.definitionFit: To ASSUME a duty is to take it on yourself, the sense of shouldering a role rather than the sense of supposing something.

clue.text: Soprano has desire to be impressively smart

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for soprano on a choral score
a wish is a thing desired

explanation.surface: An opera singer who wants to look glamorous.
explanation.walkthrough: The four choral voices all shorten to single letters on a score — S, A, T and B — so a clue naming any of them is usually after just the letter.
explanation.definitionFit: SWISH is British informal for smart in an expensive, eye-catching way: a swish hotel, a swish car.

clue.text: Variety of things scattered on mattress

indicators.note: Things scattered have been thrown about and no longer lie where they were put, so the letters land in a fresh order.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, the preposition counting as letters like any other word

explanation.surface: Odds and ends thrown down all over somebody's bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is the word to notice: it looks like the preposition holding the picture together, and it is two of the answer's letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An ASSORTMENT is a mixed collection of different sorts of thing, which is what a variety of things amounts to.

clue.text: Hostelries favoured by two Poles

parts.note: whatever is in is currently favoured or fashionable
the north and south poles, each written as the initial it goes by on a compass or a magnet

explanation.surface: Pubs that a couple of Polish visitors are fond of.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P on 'Poles' points at Poland, and the clue means the ends of the earth's axis instead.
explanation.definitionFit: An inn is a house offering travellers lodging and drink, so 'hostelries' is the same old-fashioned idea in the plural.

clue.text: Cheapen degree, dear when reviewed

parts.note: angles and temperatures are often written with deg, the clipped form of degree, as in 90 deg

indicators.note: reviewed, read as re-viewed, means looked at again in a new way, so the letters of dear are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone's degree, once precious, is cheapened when looked at again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheapen' is the verb that defines; 'degree, dear' looks like an address to a loved one but supplies DEG and the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To degrade something is to lower it in quality, status or value, which is to cheapen it.

clue.text: Some bubbly, cheese and tropical fruits

indicators.note: Asking for some of a thing asks for part of it, and the part wanted is a run of letters lying inside the words that follow.

parts.note: seven letters in a row, beginning inside the first word and running straight across the comma

explanation.surface: Champagne, cheese and fruit laid out for guests at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: A comma reads to the eye as a stop, which is exactly why a setter puts the join of a hidden answer on top of one.
explanation.definitionFit: LYCHEES are the small sweet white-fleshed fruits, grown across the tropics, that come in a rough pink shell.
